background.definition: Urticaria is the rapid appearance of pruritic, blanching, and erythematous skin wheals representing dermal vasodilation and edema. Angioedema involves localized edema of the deeper dermis and subcutaneous tissues with a relatively normal skin appearance; it usually involves the face, tongue, extremities, or genitalia.

list.listitem: Urticaria occurs alone in 50% of cases, angioedema and urticaria coexist in 40% of cases, and angioedema alone accounts for 10% of cases.
Urticaria accounts for 5% of all cutaneous drug reactions.
The incidence of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (ACEI)-induced angioedema may be up to 0.68%, and may occur at the start of therapy or after many years of use.

The incidence of angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB)-associated angioedema does not differ from placebo. Less than 10% of patients with ACEI-associated angioedema develop angioedema with subsequent use of an ARB.
Urticaria affects 15% to 25% of the population at some point during their lifetime.
Chronic urticaria has a lifetime prevalence of 2% to 3%.
Hereditary angioedema (HAE) affects 0.0007% to 0.01% of the population.
Chronic urticaria and angioedema, although rarely life-threatening, can cause a negative impact on quality of life comparable to that of severe coronary artery disease.
Nearly one third of individuals with chronic urticaria suffer from an anxiety disorder (predominantly agoraphobia).
Acute urticaria or angioedema is most commonly caused by a reaction to food, medication, or viral infection.
Common causative medications include ACEI, NSAIDs, antibiotics, and antiepileptics.
Chronic urticaria is most commonly idiopathic and may be autoimmune.
Physical urticarias have many potential triggers including cold, heat, cholinergic, exercise, dermatographism, delayed pressure, solar, or aquagenic.
Urticarial vasculitis is a possible cause.
Acquired C1-esterase inhibitor (C1-INH) deficiency is related to autoimmune and lymphoproliferative disorders which can cause antibodies to C1-INH.

Patients with hereditary angioedema (HAE) may have C1-INH deficiency. HAE1 (with low antigenic and functional C1-INH levels) and HAE2 (with normal/elevated C1-INH antigenic level but with low functional level) comprise two types of C1-INH deficiency.
Hereditary angioedema (HAE) rarely presents with normal antigenic and functional C1-INH.
Urticaria is caused by mast cell activation leading to release of histamine and other inflammatory mediators, resulting in increased vasodilation and vascular permeability in the papillary dermis.
Angioedema occurs when inflammatory mediators lead to a localized increase in vascular permeability in the submucosa, reticular dermis, and subcutaneous tissues.
Maternal dietary antigen avoidance is of uncertain benefit in the prevention of atopic disease, and may adversely affect infant nutrition.

Prophylaxis with plasma-derived C1-esterase inhibitor (C1-INH) or, alternatively, fresh frozen plasma (FFP) is indicated prior to procedures for patients with hereditary angioedema (HAE). If unavailable, consider danazol or tranexamic acid. C

For recurrent attacks (>12 attacks/year or occurring for >24 days/year), prophylaxis with C1-INH, kallikrein inhibitors (berotralstat and lanadelumab), danazol,B androgens, and tranexamic acid appear to be effective in preventing HAE attacks. C

Consider urticaria in patients presenting with rapid onset, transient, pruritic, erythematous, edematous plaques of the trunk, extremities, or face; angioedema presents as localized soft tissue edema with relatively normal overlying skin of the face, tongue, extremities, or genitalia. C
A detailed history is the most effective diagnostic approach for chronic urticaria, and extensive empiric laboratory testing is usually not needed. C
Guide the diagnostic testing for urticaria with or without angioedema by clues in the history and physical. C

For patients who have recurrent isolated angioedema or a family history of angioedema, order testing for C1-esterase inhibitor (C1-INH) deficiency with a serum C4, C1-INH antigenic level, C1-INH functional level, and C1q.C

Differential.Differential_Features: Skin changes more persistent and more peripherally distributed than urticaria
Bullae rather than wheals or nonpitting edema
Reddish brown spots on skin that form hives when skin is stroked

list.listitem: Urticaria is the rapid appearance of pruritic, blanching, erythematous skin wheals representing dermal vasodilation and edema. It can be acute, lasting hours to days, or chronic, with daily symptoms lasting longer than 6 weeks. It can also be episodic, appearing acutely over a period of hours to days and presenting intermittently over months to years.

Angioedema involves localized edema of the deeper dermis and subcutaneous tissues with a relatively normal skin appearance. It is typically not pruritic but can be painful. It often involves the face, tongue, extremities, or genitalia and can involve visceral organs. Like urticaria, it can be acute, chronic, or episodic.

Consider urticaria in patients presenting with rapid onset, transient, pruritic, erythematous, edematous plaques of the trunk, extremities, or face; angioedema presents as localized soft tissue edema with relatively normal overlying skin of the face, tongue, extremities, or genitalia.

Detailed history is the most important diagnostic step for patients with urticaria and/or angioedema. Photographs taken by the patient are extremely helpful too. Symptom diaries may help characterize episodes better and identify potential triggers.
Characterize duration of symptoms and ask about associated symptoms such as arthralgia, fever, respiratory symptoms, or abdominal pain.

Other associated conditions include autoimmune disorders, a family history of angioedema or tendency toward atopy, malignancy, and potential allergic triggers including food, contact, or environmental allergens. Allergic triggers should cause a reproducible reaction within 60 minutes of exposure.

Common culprits include angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (ACEI), nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and aspirin. Drug reactions can develop spontaneously even after a patient has been on a medication for many years.

Other important findings from the history and physical include known physical triggers or the presence of dermatographism on examination. Consider provocative testing for other suspected physical triggers, such as cold or water.
A normal C4 level may help rule out angioedema during a suspected attack.
Select diagnostic tests based on clues from the history rather than extensive testing for all patients.
The literature regarding accuracy of specific diagnostic tests is limited, and recommended diagnostic tests are generally on the basis of expert consensus.
See and for implementation of diagnostic strategies and for the rationale behind different diagnostic tests.
Detailed history is essential. Extensive laboratory testing does not add to the diagnostic yield, so diagnostic studies should be guided by history and examination.

Further work-up may be indicated, such as skin prick testing, CBC, urinalysis, ESR, cryoglobulins, thryroid studies/antibodies, challenge testing for physical urticarias, skin biopsy, autologous serum skin testing, or complement studies.

The 2021 British Association of Dermatologists (BAD) guidelines for the management of chronic urticaria, based on low-quality evidence, recommend considering ordering total IgE levels for patients with inadequate response to H1-antihistamines and montelukast who are being considered for second-line therapies like omalizumab or cyclosporine. Retrospective studies suggest that patients with high total IgE levels may respond earlier and more robustly to omalizumab, whereas patients with normal total IgE levels may respond better to cyclosporine.
See diagnostic algorithms in (angioedema) and (urticaria).
Key priciples of management include identification and avoidance of triggers, patient education, and a personalized therapeutic plan. C

H1-antihistamines are the treatment of choice for acute and chronic urticaria and/or angioedema, with preference for the improved side effect profile of second generation nonsedating H1-antihistamines. A
For acute urticaria, the addition of oral corticosteroids to oral antihistamines is of uncertain benefit. B
Other adjunctive agents for urticaria include the montelukast (leukotriene receptor antagonist), cyclosporine,B and omalizumab. A
Treat hereditary angioedema (HAE) with C1-esterase inhibitor (C1-INH) replacement, kallikrein inhibitors, bradykinin B2 receptor blockers, danazol,B attenuated androgens, or tranexamic acid ().C

The 2021 British Association of Dermatologists (BAD) guidelines for the management of chronic urticaria recommend considering assessing disease activity and impact using validated scoring tools (eg, Dermatology Life Quality Index [DLQI], Urticaria Activity Score 7 [UAS7], Angioedema Activity Score [AAS], Urticaria Control Test [UCT]), offering patients and families educational materials (https://www.skinhealthinfo.org.uk/a-z-conditions-treatments), offering access to services to evaluate and treat mental health disorders, considering topical antipruritic medications like menthol-containing emollients, telling patients to avoid identified triggers or precipitating factors like medications and physical exposures (eg, sun, cold, pressure, etc.), and stopping angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (ACEI) in patients with angioedema without urticaria.

H1-antihistamines are the initial treatment of choice. FDA-approved first generation H1-antihistamine agents include diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine, doxepin, brompheniramine, cyproheptadine, and clemastine. Second generation H1-antihistamines (loratadine, desloratadine, fexofenadine, cetirizine, and levocetirizine) are preferred over first generation agents because of equal efficacy with improved side effect profile.

For chronic spontaneous (idiopathic) urticaria, a Cochrane review in 2014, based on low-quality evidence, found similar efficacy between different H1-antihistamines. Cetirizine 10mg daily appears effective for short- and intermediate-term complete suppression of urticaria. Levocetirizine 20mg daily appears effective short-term, while levocetirizine 5mg daily appears efficacious for intermediate-term urticaria suppression. Rates of adverse events were similar between treatment and placebo arms of the involved studies. There was insufficient evidence to assess the effects of H1 antihistamines on quality of life.

Maximizing the dose of a single second generation H1-antihistamine, up to three to four times recommended dose (eg, cetirizine 30-40mg/day), is preferred rather than mixing different types of antihistamines (eg, cetrizine with hydroxyzine).

For patients with chronic urticaria not adequately controlled with high-dose second generation H1-antihistamine (eg, cetirizine), the 2021 BAD guidelines suggest switching to another second generation H1-antihistamine (eg, fexofenadine) with the goal of titrating up to four-fold the licensed dose.

A Cochrane review in 2012 found four small RCTs with uncertain to high risk of bias evaluating H2 receptor antagonists in patients with urticaria. They found the addition of an H2-antihistamine (eg, famotidine or cimetidine) to diphenhydramine may improve symptom resolution, but caution the evidence is very limited to make general recommendations.

Intravenous (IV) cetirizine for the treatment of acute urticaria with severe itching is an effective alternative to IV diphenhydramine and demonstrated less sedation and other adverse effects in a randomized noninferiority trial.

Based on a small RCT involving 43 patients in the emergency department, systemic corticosteroids (prednisone) may be a beneficial adjunct to oral antihistamines for acute urticaria. However, a newer study that randomized 100 adults in the emergency department with acute urticaria (with no angioedema or anaphylaxis) found no additional benefit when prednisone 40mg daily for 4 days was added to oral levocetirizine 5mg daily for 5 days. On telephone follow up, 62% treated with antihistamine/steroid and 76% receiving antihistamine/placebo were asymptomatic, with no significant difference between the two study arms.
Despite absence of clinical trial evidence of effectiveness, corticosteroids are also commonly used for flare-ups and refractory chronic urticaria.

listitem.strong: Monoclonal antibodies and tyrosine kinase inhibitors

list.listitem: Omalizumab (a monoclonal antibody against IgE) at doses of 300 and 600 mg improves urticaria symptoms over four weeks in patients refractory to antihistamines. A multinational drug survival cohort study found omalizumab to be safe and effective for chronic urticaria, with the main reason of treatment discontinuation being well-controlled disease. A cost-effectiveness analysis also found omalizumab 300mg to be cost-effective for H1 antihistamine-refractory chronic spontaneous urticaria in the US, using a willingness to pay threshold of $150,000 per QALY.

The monoclonal antibody lanadelumab (a plasma kallikrein inhibitor) was evaluated in an RCT of 125 patients aged ≥12 years with hereditary angioedema (HAE). At 26 weeks, patients had fewer attacks of HAE when dosed at 150 mg every 4 weeks, 300 mg every 4 weeks, or 300 mg every 2 weeks compared to placebo (NNT = 1.46-1.74). Adverse events were minimal in all treatment groups.

An RCT identified 160 patients with inadequate response to anti-histamines and randomized them to 3 different doses of rilzabrutinib or placebo. After 3 months, significant reductions in itch and hive severity scores were seen for the highest dose (400 mg tid) compared with placebo.

A trial randomized 925 patients with chronic urticaria who failed antihistamines to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor remibrutinib 25 mg twice daily or placebo. At 12 weeks patients receiving remibrutinib were more likely to have a clinical response (50% vs 25%, p < 0.001, NNT = 4). Improvement on the 42 point UAS7 score was about 6 to 7 points greater in the treatment group, a difference that is probably clinically significant. It is noteworthy that in this trial and the trial of rilzabrutinib, patients in the placebo group saw fairly large improvements in their score of 12 to 14 points on the 42 point scale.

Donidalorsen reduces prekallikrein expression. A trial randomized 90 patients to donidalorsen every 4 weeks, every 8 weeks, or placebo and evaluated the reduction in attack rate between weeks 1 and 25. A greater than 50% reduction in attacks was seen in 42% in the 4 week group, 19% in the 8 week group and 6% in the placebo group.
A small trial evaluated CRISPR therapy in 20 patients compared with 6 who received placebo. Active therapy reduced the attack rate by 75%.

Montelukast, a leukotriene receptor antagonist, is another first-line agent for adults and children with chronic urticaria who have not achieved adequate symptom control despite high doses of second generation H1-antihistamines.
Tranexamic acid is the preferred second-line agent for patients with angioedema without urticaria.

Immunomodulating agents (eg, cyclosporine, omalizumab) are recommended for treatment-refractory cases of chronic urticaria. Consider checking total IgE level to help predict response to immunomodulatory treatment since patients with high total IgE levels may respond earlier and more robustly to omalizumab, whereas patients with normal total IgE levels may respond better to cyclosporine.
Only low-quality studies support alternative adjunctive agents such as tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil.

For acute treatment of C1-INH deficiency, plasma derived C1-INH, recombinant C1-INH, kallikrein inhibitors, and bradykinin B2 receptor blockers (eg, icatibant) are more effective than placebo. The FAST-2 trial demonstrated that icatibant leads to symptom relief more quickly than tranexamic acid (2h vs 12h, p < .001). No other studies have compared drugs head-to-head for acute treatment.

A Cochrane review evaluating 15 RCTs enrolling 912 participants found C1-Ithat NH, kallikrein inhibitors (berotralstat and lanadelumab), and danazol to bwereective in preventing HAE attacks, while C1-INH and lanadelumab appear to decrease the severity of breakthrough attacks. Additionally, avoralstat (another kallikrein inhibitor), berotralstat, and C1-INH appear to improve quality of life and do not increase adverse events.

Icatibant, a selective bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist, was more effective than standard therapy of glucocorticoids and antihistamines producing complete resolution of edema in patients with ACEI-induced angioedema. This was a phase 2 clinical trial in 30 patients. Icatibant is FDA approved for use in HAE since 2011.

Scant evidence guides therapy of acquired angioedema. Anti-fibrinolytics may be more effective for acquired angioedema than for HAE. However, C1-INH replacement may be less efficacious due to antibodies. Treatment of any underlying lymphoproliferative disorder or autoimmune disease may improve symptoms.
Stress management may be helpful for chronic urticaria.
Anecdotally, topical treatment with cooling antipruritic lotions containing 1% to 4% menthol may be soothing.
Advise patient to avoid identified triggers.
For exercise-induced urticaria, patients should avoid eating for 4 hours prior to exercise.
Patients with chronic urticaria or angioedema taking a medication suspected to cause their symptoms should undergo a trial off the medication for several weeks.
Treatment of associated conditions may improve symptoms.
For HAE, patients should avoid ACEI, estrogen, and plasminogen activators.
Empiric 3- to 6-month antihistamine treatment is common, but if the patient presents with prolonged symptoms, a 6- to 12-month treatment course with gradual withdrawal is advised.

Expert guidelines suggest consideration of referral to an allergist or dermatologist for the following situations:
A severe episode of acute urticaria or angioedema without a defined trigger, or if in need of diagnostic confirmation of a suspected trigger Chronic urticaria/angioedema of more than 6 weeks' duration Suspected urticarial vasculitis or urticaria with systemic disease Recurrent angioedema without urticaria
Chronic urticaria/angioedema resolves within 1 year for one-third of patients. Symptoms improve significantly within 1 year in over half of patients. B
Prognosis is best for those with idiopathic urticaria and worst for those with physical urticaria. B
Chronic urticaria often improves in pregnancy.
Prescribe all medications cautiously in pregnancy, including antihistamines, with discussion of risks and benefits. Use the lowest effective dose of loratadine, cetirizine, or chlorpheniramine.

Avoid prescribing antihistamines during lactation if possible, but risks and benefits should be weighed. If an antihistamine is prescribed, use the lowest effective dose of loratadine or cetirizine, and avoid chlorpheniramine.

The clinical course of HAE varies in pregnancy. Consult a specialist for assistance in management. Plasma derived C1-INH is recommended for acute treatment and prophylaxis. Alternatively, tranexamic acid may be used after weighing risks versus benefits, but should be avoided in the first trimester due to possible teratogenicity and fetal death. Danazol is contraindicated during pregnancy. Bradykinin 2 receptor antagonists, kallikrein antagonists, and recombinant C1-INH have not been studied in pregnancy.
Plasma derived C1-INH is preferred while breastfeeding.
Household members of children with food allergies report urticaria and angioedema as the most common presenting symptoms after an exposure.
A thorough history and physical typically identifies a diagnosis of urticaria in children; perform further diagnostic testing only if suggested by the history and physical.
Physical triggers such as pressure or cold are the most commonly diagnosed triggers in children with chronic urticaria.
If children have associated systemic symptoms, skin biopsy should be considered. Henoch-Schonlein purpura is the most common cause of acute vasculitic urticaria in children.
There may be an association between chronic urticaria and thyroid autoimmunity or celiac disease in children.
Avoidance of triggers is a key component of therapy.
H1-antihistamines are the treatment of choice, preferably second generation nonsedating antihistamines.
Adjunctive agents may include leukotriene inhibitors, short-term systemic corticosteroids, tranexamic acid, and omalizumab (children older than 7 years).
Consider screening children with a family history of HAE. Children with the disorder commonly present with abdominal pain alone.
Plasma derived C1-INH effectively treats acute attacks of HAE and prevents recurrence when given prophylactically. Avoid long term use of attenuated androgens due to concern for adverse effects.
One half to two thirds of children with chronic urticaria will have remission or resolution of symptoms within 60 to 74 months.

feature.caption: Diagnosis of Urticaria/Angioedema Subtypes.
feature.feature_body:
Subtype of Urticaria/Angioedema Features of History and Physical Diagnostic Tests
Allergic urticaria/angioedema Reproducible reaction within 60 min after exposure to particular food, contact, or environmental allergen Skin prick testing for specific allergens, trial of avoidance of suspected trigger with recurrence of symptoms on reintroduction
Medication-induced urticaria/angioedema Taking medication known to cause urticaria/angioedema such as ACEI, NSAID, antibiotic, or antiepileptic
Chronic idiopathic urticaria/angioedema Duration of >6 wk; no identifiable trigger Normal
Autoimmune urticaria Associated autoimmune disease Thyroid function, thyroid antibodies may be abnormal; autologous serum skin test may be positive (this test is still investigational)
Physical urticaria History suggests reproducible physical trigger; examine for dermatographism or challenge with specific trigger such as ice cube test for cold urticaria or water immersion for aquagenic urticaria Cryoglobulins may be present in cold urticaria
Urticarial vasculitis Associated systemic symptoms such as fever, arthralgia, duration of lesions >24 h, painful skin lesions Skin biopsy shows vasculitis; CBC may show neutrophilia; ESR may be elevated; UA may be abnormal
Hereditary angioedema Recurrent isolated angioedema presenting early in life; symptoms may involve laryngeal or visceral angioedema causing respiratory distress or abdominal pain; may have family history of angioedema HAE1: Low C1-INH antigenic and functional levels; low C4; normal C1qHAE2: Normal/increased C1-INH antigenic level; low C1-INH functional level; low C4; normal C1qHAE with normal C1-INH: normal C1-INH antigenic and functional levels; normal C4; normal C1q; FXII mutation may be present
Acquired C1-INH deficiency Recurrent isolated angioedema presenting later in life; may have associated lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease Low C1-INH antigenic and functional levels; low C4; low C1q
Data from Lang et al. and Powell et al.
